mainTopic: Doubtful נזירות vows that depend on a son being born, and what happens when one נזירות term interrupts another
overview: The amud opens by finishing a question about a friend who answers 'and I' when someone vows to be a נזיר once a certain person has a son. If that person is not there, does the friend mean his own future son, or is he saying he loves that person just as much? The גמרא finds no answer and leaves it as תיבעי. Then a new משנה teaches how to order two נזירות terms, one starting now and one starting when a son is born. If he mentioned his own term first, he finishes it and only then counts the son's term. If he mentioned the son's term first, he pauses his own, counts the son's, and then finishes his own. In the גמרא, רבא asks whether a 100-day נזירות can start now if a 30-day term will interrupt it after 20 days. The גמרא asks why רבא didn't ask about a short term instead, and answers that his question grew out of an earlier question. That earlier question is laid out on the next amud.

steps.title: Does 'And I' mean the friend's son or his own son?
steps.stepSummary: Someone vows to be a נזיר when a certain person has a son. His friend hears and says 'and I'. The original person is not there. Does the friend mean when he himself has a son, or when that person has a son?
steps.simpleTranslation: If it were in front of him, it would be embarrassing, so 'and I' would surely mean that person's son. But if someone said, 'I am a נזיר when so-and-so has a son,' and his friend heard and said 'And I,' what is the law? Do we say that since it was not in front of so-and-so, the friend means himself, a son of his own? Or perhaps he is saying, 'I love him just as you do'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the friend's 'and I' means when the person who will have the son is not there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the person is present, saying 'I mean my own son' would be insulting, so we assume the friend means that person's son. When he is not present, there is no embarrassment, so maybe the friend means his own son. Or maybe he still means 'I care about this person as much as you do.'

keyTerms.meaning: The matter is embarrassing for him
I love him as you do

phrases.english: the matter is embarrassing for him,
phrases.notes: This finishes the earlier case: in front of the person, saying 'I mean my own son' would be embarrassing.

phrases.english: If one said: "I am hereby a nazir
when so-and-so will have a son,"
and his friend heard and said: "And I,"
what is the law?
Do we say: since it was not in his presence,
he is speaking about himself,
phrases.notes: He means: I'll be a נזיר when I have a son of my own.

phrases.english: or perhaps this is what he is saying to him:
I love him just as you do.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי אָמְרִינַן: שֶׁלֹּא בְּפָנָיו, אַנַּפְשֵׁיהּ קָאָמַר, אוֹ דִילְמָא הָכִי קָאָמַר לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion of 'and I' cases, now asking about when the person is not present.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the friend's 'and I' means 'when I have a son' or 'when so-and-so has a son' when so-and-so is not present.

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: No answer is found, so the question is left open.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand as a question.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the question without an answer: תיבעי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both readings of the friend's words make sense, and the גמרא finds no source to decide between them. So the law in this case stays doubtful.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it remain a question; unresolved

phrases.english: Let it remain a question.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the question of step 1 without resolving it.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The meaning of 'and I' said not in the person's presence is left as an open doubt.

steps.title: Own נזירות first, then the son's
steps.stepSummary: The משנה: someone said 'I am a נזיר, and a נזיר when I have a son.' He started his own term, and then a son was born. He finishes his own term first, then counts the son's term.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If one said, 'I am hereby a נזיר, and a נזיר when I will have a son,' and he began counting his own term, and then a son was born to him, he completes his own term and afterward counts the term for his son.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It teaches the order of two נזירות terms when he mentioned his own term first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His own נזירות was said first and already started, so it simply continues to the end. Only then does the נזירות for the son begin.

phrases.english: MISHNA: "I am hereby a nazir,
and a nazir when I will have a son,"
he began counting his own term,
and afterward a son was born to him,
he completes his own term,

phrases.aramaic: וְאַחַר כָּךְ מוֹנֶה אֶת שֶׁל בְּנוֹ.
phrases.english: and afterward counts the term of his son.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ ״הֲרֵינִי נָזִיר, וְנָזִיר כְּשֶׁיִּהְיֶה לִי בֵּן״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה, separate from the unresolved question before it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When his own נזירות was mentioned first, he finishes it and then counts the son's term.

steps.title: Son's נזירות said first, so he pauses his own
steps.stepSummary: If he said the son's נזירות first ('a נזיר when I have a son, and a נזיר'), and the son was born in the middle of his own term, he pauses his own term, counts the son's, and then finishes his own.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said, 'I am hereby a נזיר when I will have a son, and a נזיר,' and he began counting his own term, and then a son was born to him, he sets aside his own term, counts the term for his son, and afterward completes his own.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the opposite order and gets a different result: now the son's term interrupts his own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The only change is which נזירות he mentioned first. Since he put the son's term first, it takes priority when the son is born, even in the middle of his own term. This teaches that a נזירות term can be paused and finished later.
steps.whatToRemember: Order of words matters: own term first means finish it; son's term first means pause your own for the son's, then finish your own.
steps.confusionAlert: In both cases he actually started his own term first. The difference comes only from the order in which he said the two vows.

phrases.english: "I am hereby a nazir when I will have a son, and a nazir,"
he began counting his own term
and afterward a son was born to him,
he sets aside his own term,
and counts the term of his son,
and afterward completes his own term.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The reverse case of step 3, with the opposite result.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When the son's נזירות was mentioned first, he pauses his own term for the son's, then completes his own.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a נזירות can be interrupted and resumed, which is the basis for רבא's question next.

steps.title: Can a 100-day נזירות start now if a 30-day term will interrupt it?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks: someone said 'I am a נזיר starting in 20 days, and from now for 100 days.' Does the 100-day term start now and get paused after 20 days? Or does it not start until later?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: If one said, 'I am hereby a נזיר starting after twenty days, and from now for one hundred days,' what is the law? Since the hundred days can't be finished within the twenty, maybe they do not start now? Or perhaps, since he will still have real hair growth at the end, they do start now?
steps.whatsHappening: In the גמרא, רבא asks a new question built on the משנה's idea of pausing one נזירות for another.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plain 30-day term must start on day 20, so the 100 days would be cut off after 20 days. One side: an unfinished start doesn't count, so the 100 days wait. Other side: after the 30-day pause he still has 80 days left, enough for real hair growth, so the 100 days can start now.

keyTerms.meaning: Hair growth, the sign of a real נזירות

phrases.english: GEMARA: Rava asked:
If one said: "I am hereby a nazir after twenty days,
phrases.notes: No number is given here, so this is a regular 30-day נזירות.

phrases.english: and from now for one hundred days," what is the law?
Since these hundred days
are not completed within the twenty,
they do not take effect,
or perhaps: since he has
hair growth at the end,
phrases.notes: After the 30-day pause, 80 days are left, which is long enough for real hair growth.

phrases.english: they do take effect.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רָבָא: אָמַר ״הֲרֵינִי נָזִיר לְאַחַר עֶשְׂרִים יוֹם, וּמֵעַכְשָׁיו מֵאָה יוֹם״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the משנה's rule that one נזירות can interrupt another.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a long נזירות starts now if it will be interrupted before finishing, given enough hair growth remains afterward.

steps.title: Why not ask about a short נזירות?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבא didn't ask about a shorter term, where after the pause less than 30 days would be left.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him ask instead about a short נזירות!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges how רבא built his question: a short term seems like the more interesting case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With 100 days, plenty of hair growth is left after the pause. With a short term, the leftover days would be too few for real hair growth, so that would be the harder test. Why did רבא pick the 100-day case?

phrases.english: But let him ask
about a short nazirite term!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the way רבא set up his question in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's choice of a 100-day term for his question.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A short term, where too little hair growth is left after the pause, seems the more obvious case to ask about.

steps.title: One question grew out of another
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבא's question came out of an earlier question, and begins to lay that out.
steps.simpleTranslation: He is asking one question as an outgrowth of another.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge and sets up the next part, where it will show the earlier question that led to רבא's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's 100-day case was not his starting point. It came as a follow-up to another question, and that explains why it is worded this way. The details come right after this line.

keyTerms.meaning: He asks, it is a question for him

phrases.english: One out of the other
he is asking:

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲדָא מִגּוֹ חֲדָא קָא מִיבַּעְיָא לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6 and prepares the next part.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the background of the question
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבא should have asked the more obvious short-term case.
